chapters.title: Chapter 5: Scaling Playbook: Growing AUM Without Killing the Edge

lessons.title: When to Stop Scaling: Recognizing Diminishing Returns

children.text: This chapter has given three real ways to scale: diversify across strategies, stratify across segments and instruments, and correctly diagnose which lever actually fits your constraint. All three eventually run out of room. This closing lesson is about recognizing that point before it recognizes you.

Each additional genuinely independent sleeve added to a portfolio tends to improve portfolio-level risk-adjusted return by a smaller amount than the sleeve before it, a standard result in portfolio construction generally, not something unique to capacity-constrained strategies. The first new sleeve you add is usually the most obviously complementary idea available. Every one after that is, almost by definition, a little less obviously complementary than the last.

body.title: Illustrative Portfolio Sharpe as Sleeves Are Added

cells: The most genuinely complementary strategy or instrument is usually the second one added, not the fifth
Independent ideas are a finite resource
There are only so many genuinely uncorrelated, low-overlap signals available at any point in time
Every sleeve adds fixed operational cost
Monitoring, infrastructure, and team bandwidth scale with the number of sleeves, regardless of how small each one's contribution becomes

children.text: There is an old, uncomfortable truism in markets: in a crisis, correlations go to one. Low normal-time correlation between your sleeves is not a guarantee during genuine systemic stress. If the fund as a whole needs to cut risk sharply, because of redemptions, a risk-limit breach, or a shock in one sleeve spilling into the fund's overall book, every sleeve can get sold together at once, regardless of how independent their historical returns looked.

body.text: This is the Chapter 3 crowding mechanism turned inward. The August 2007 example showed unrelated funds getting hit together by a shared factor exposure. The same forced-selling logic can just as easily apply within a single fund's own multiple sleeves, if the trigger for deleveraging is the fund's overall risk budget rather than any single sleeve's own signal breaking down.

children.text: Practical Signals That It Is Time to Stop

body.title: Before Adding Another Sleeve, Ask
steps: Does the next candidate strategy's estimated marginal contribution to portfolio Sharpe clear a threshold I set in advance, rather than just looking attractive on its own?
Do I actually have the monitoring and operational bandwidth to run one more sleeve properly, on top of everything already running?
Has the correlation estimate I am relying on been tested across a real stress period, not just calm, benign markets?
Am I adding this sleeve because it improves the portfolio, or because I want a bigger AUM number to raise more capital, the exact trap Chapter 1 warned about?

body.text: Every scaling lever in this chapter eventually runs out of genuinely independent room, and normal-time correlation numbers understate how connected your sleeves really are once markets get stressed. Knowing when to stop adding is as much a part of the scaling playbook as knowing how to add in the first place.

points: Each additional genuinely independent sleeve typically improves portfolio-level risk-adjusted return by less than the one before it, a standard diminishing-returns pattern in portfolio construction.
The pool of genuinely independent, low-overlap strategies and instruments is finite, and every additional sleeve adds real operational cost regardless of how small its contribution becomes.
Normal-time correlation between sleeves can understate true dependence during a systemic shock, since a fund-wide deleveraging event can force otherwise independent sleeves to sell together at once.
A short checklist, marginal Sharpe threshold, operational bandwidth, stress-tested correlation, and honest motive, is a practical way to decide when scaling has stopped paying for itself.
